title: Module Header: Three Identities in the Hockey Stick Hierarchy
content: The module docstring states the open question ('Generalize the hockey stick identity to multi-dimensional sums') and previews the three identities proved: the 1D hockey stick (already known), the parallel Vandermonde (new intermediate result), and the 2D hockey stick (the target). The dependency graph is explicit: parallel Vandermonde is the technical core, 2D hockey stick follows by composition with the 1D result. The `open Finset BigOperators` makes range, sum, and ∑ notation available throughout, standard for Lean 4 combinatorics proofs in Mathlib.
mathContext:
The three-identity hierarchy:
$$\text{1D: } \sum_{i=0}^n \binom{i+k}{k} = \binom{n+k+1}{k+1}$$
$$\text{Parallel Vandermonde: } \sum_{i+j=n} \binom{i+a}{a}\binom{j+b}{b} = \binom{n+a+b+1}{a+b+1}$$
$$\text{2D: } \sum_{i+j \leq n} \binom{i+a}{a}\binom{j+b}{b} = \binom{n+a+b+2}{a+b+2}$$
The 2D identity is essentially $\sum_{m=0}^{n}(\text{parallel Vandermonde at }m)$, i.e., applying the 1D hockey stick to the parallel Vandermonde result.

title: Summary: 12 Theorems, Nested Induction Architecture
content: The file summary enumerates the three main parts: (I) parallel Vandermonde by nested induction on (b, n), (II) 2D hockey stick as a two-step composition, (III) special cases and concrete verification. The key insights documented are (1) the parallel Vandermonde satisfies the same recurrence as simplicial numbers — so the proof reduces to matching two sequences that obey the same recurrence with the same initial conditions; (2) Pascal on S_{b+1} decomposes each term into two IH applications; (3) the 2D hockey stick is literally `hockey_stick ∘ parallel_vandermonde`; and (4) natural number subtraction issues are avoided by careful sum splitting. The `end ArithmeticSeriesOQ02OQ02` closes the namespace.
mathContext:
The full proof chain: $\mathtt{simplicial}(k, n) = \binom{n+k}{k}$ (definition) $\to$ $\mathtt{simplicial\_succ}$ (Pascal) $\to$ $\mathtt{hockey\_stick}$ $\to$ $\mathtt{parallel\_vandermonde}$ (nested induction) $\to$ $\mathtt{hockey\_stick\_2d}$ (2-line composition). Total: 12 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

The recurrence-matching insight: if two sequences $f(b,n)$ and $g(b,n)$ satisfy the same Pascal-like recurrence and agree on all base cases $(b=0$ and $n=0)$, then $f \equiv g$ by induction — no explicit bijection needed.
prerequisites: all preceding theorems in the file

title: Simplicial Numbers
content: Defines the $k$-th simplicial number $S_k(n) = \binom{n+k}{k}$, which counts the number of lattice points in a $k$-dimensional simplex of side length $n$. For $k=0$ these are the constant $1$, for $k=1$ the natural numbers, for $k=2$ the triangular numbers $\binom{n+2}{2}$, and for $k=3$ the tetrahedral numbers. The definition is self-contained, depending only on `Nat.choose`.

title: Base Cases with @[simp]
content: Two base cases tagged `@[simp]` for automatic simplification: $S_0(n) = 1$ (the 0-dimensional simplex is a point) and $S_k(0) = 1$ (any simplex of side length 0 has one vertex). The first uses `Nat.choose_zero_right` and the second uses `Nat.choose_self`, reflecting the combinatorial identities $\binom{n}{0} = 1$ and $\binom{k}{k} = 1$.

title: Pascal Recurrence for Simplicial Numbers
content: The fundamental recurrence $S_{k+1}(n+1) = S_{k+1}(n) + S_k(n+1)$ translates Pascal's identity $\binom{m+1}{r+1} = \binom{m}{r+1} + \binom{m}{r}$ into the simplicial number framework. The `ring` tactic handles the index arithmetic, and `linarith` applies Mathlib's `Nat.choose_succ_succ`. This recurrence is the engine of the nested induction in the main proof.

title: 1D Hockey Stick Identity
content: The classical hockey stick (Christmas stocking) identity: $\sum_{i=0}^{n} S_k(i) = S_{k+1}(n)$. The proof is a clean one-line induction: the successor case peels off the last term via `sum_range_succ`, applies the induction hypothesis, and closes with the Pascal recurrence. This identity gets its name from the pattern in Pascal's triangle: summing entries along a diagonal gives the entry one step further along the next diagonal.

title: Parallel Vandermonde Convolution Identity
content: The central result: $\sum_{i+j=n} S_a(i) \cdot S_b(j) = S_{a+b+1}(n)$. This is a convolution identity stating that the convolution of the $a$-th and $b$-th simplicial sequences yields the $(a+b+1)$-th simplicial sequence. The proof uses nested induction: outer induction on $b$ (base case reduces to the hockey stick) and inner induction on $n$. The key step applies Pascal's recurrence to decompose $S_{b+1}(n+1-i)$ into two terms, splitting the sum into parts resolvable by the inner and outer induction hypotheses. The final combination uses the simplicial recurrence `simplicial_succ`.

title: Sum Decomposition via Pascal
content: The critical step of the induction: applying Pascal's identity $S_{b+1}(n+1-i) = S_{b+1}(n-i) + S_b(n+1-i)$ inside the sum, then using `sum_add_distrib` to split into two sums. The subtraction index arithmetic $n + 1 - i = (n - i) + 1$ is verified by `omega`, which handles natural number arithmetic safely (avoiding the pitfalls of natural number subtraction). This is the technical heart of the proof.
mathContext: $\sum_i S_a(i) \cdot S_{b+1}(n+1-i) = \sum_i S_a(i) \cdot S_{b+1}(n-i) + \sum_i S_a(i) \cdot S_b(n+1-i)$

title: 2D Hockey Stick: Composition of 1D Results
content: The 2D hockey stick identity is proved in just two lines: `simp_rw [parallel_vandermonde]` replaces each inner sum $\sum_{i+j=m} S_a(i) S_b(j)$ by $S_{a+b+1}(m)$, then `hockey_stick` closes the resulting 1D sum. This elegant composition demonstrates how the parallel Vandermonde acts as a bridge between dimensions: it converts a 2D sum into a 1D sum that the hockey stick already handles.

title: Special Cases and Computational Verification
content: Three verification results: `parallel_vandermonde_left` shows that setting $a=0$ reduces to the 1D hockey stick (since $S_0(i) = 1$), providing a sanity check on the general identity. The `native_decide` checks verify $S_2(2) = 6$ (the 2-simplex with 6 lattice points) and $S_3(2) = 10$ (confirming the Vandermonde convolution at small values). These concrete computations ground the abstract identities in tangible numbers.
